y-m-52-01.title: Is the result the same if we swap the order?
y-m-52-01.goal: Learn that getting the same result for one input is not evidence for 'always the same,' and refute the claim by finding inputs where the order changes the result.
y-m-52-01.material:
There are two calculating machines. Machine f doubles the input and adds 1 (f(x)=2x+1), and machine g squares the input (g(x)=x²). The input can be any real number.
If you connect them as 'f then g,' the result is g(f(x)); if you connect them as 'g then f,' the result is f(g(x)). Minseo said, “For any two machines, the result is the same even if you swap the order. It works for our machines too when I put in 0. f then g: f(0)=1, g(1)=1. g then f: g(0)=0, f(0)=1.”
y-m-52-01.thinking.0: Decide whether one example is enough to generalize
y-m-52-01.thinking.2: Tell apart the special inputs where the two expressions happen to be equal
y-m-52-01.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level for production assignment; the curriculum does not set a grade for it. It assumes students who have already studied the functions unit of high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-52-01.prereq.1: The meaning of the composite function f(g(x)) and finding its values (functions unit)
y-m-52-01.prereq.2: Calculating with linear and quadratic functions
y-m-52-01.s.s1.prompt: Minseo checked that both orders give 1 for the input 0. What can we say from this check?
y-m-52-01.s.s1.hint.0: Make a table that calculates the two orders separately, and try the inputs 0, 1, and -1.
y-m-52-01.s.s1.hint.1: Look in the table for even one cell where the two results are different.
y-m-52-01.s.s1.o.c: They match at 0, but we do not know whether they match for other inputs. We need to change the input and calculate separately.
y-m-52-01.s.s1.r.c: This shows you understand that the result for one input tells us only about that input, and you want to pick more inputs to test.
y-m-52-01.s.s1.explain: Matching at one input means they match only at that input. To check or break 'always,' you need to test other inputs too.
y-m-52-01.s.s2.prompt: Find 3 different inputs x that break Minseo's claim. (The two results g(f(x)) and f(g(x)) must be different. You may use any real number x.)
y-m-52-01.s.s2.hint.0: Apply g to the value you get by applying f first to the input x, then swap the order and calculate again.
y-m-52-01.s.s2.hint.1: Try small integers near 0 one by one and compare whether the two values are equal.
y-m-52-01.s.s2.ok.c1: The results of the two orders are different.
y-m-52-01.s.s2.fail.c1: For this input the results of the two orders are the same. Pick another input and calculate both orders again.
y-m-52-01.s.s2.explain: g(f(x))=(2x+1)²=4x²+4x+1 and f(g(x))=2x²+1. For example, for x=1 they are 9 and 3, and for x=2 they are 25 and 9, which are different. The difference of the two expressions is 2x²+4x=2x(x+2), so the only inputs where they are equal are x=0 and x=-2; every other input is a counterexample.
y-m-52-01.s.s3.prompt: What would you say to Minseo? Give a counterexample with numbers to show the claim is wrong, and add a word about the inputs where the two orders gave the same result (are there others besides 0?).
y-m-52-01.s.s3.hint.0: Pick one of the inputs you found above and write the results of the two orders side by side.
y-m-52-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you calculate and write both results of the two orders for the input you chose?
y-m-52-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain that 'it was the same at 0' and 'it is always the same' are different statements?
y-m-52-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check whether there are more inputs where they are equal before writing?
y-m-52-01.s.s3.model.0: No. If x=1, f then g gives 9 but g then f gives 3. The result can change with the order. At 0 it was just an input where they happen to be equal.
y-m-52-01.s.s3.model.1: They are not always the same. If you put in 2, you get 25 and 9, which differ. Besides 0, the input -2 also gives equal results, which is a special value where the two expressions 4x²+4x+1 and 2x²+1 meet.
y-m-52-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that finds, using the expressions, the inputs where they are equal

y-m-52-02.title: Where do the two graphs meet?
y-m-52-02.topic: Intersection of the graphs of inverse functions
y-m-52-02.goal: Refute, with a counterexample, the wrong generalization that the fact 'the graph of an inverse function is symmetric about y=x' means 'the intersection points are also on y=x,' and state the condition under which counterexamples occur.
y-m-52-02.material:
When a function f has an inverse function f⁻¹, the two graphs are symmetric about the line y=x. Jiho said, “So the points where the graphs of f and f⁻¹ meet are always on the line y=x. For example, if f(x)=2x−3, then f⁻¹(x)=(x+3)/2 and the two graphs meet at (3,3), so it's right. f(x)=x³ also meets at (0,0), (1,1), and (−1,−1).”
(Only consider functions defined for all real numbers x. Let's call the line y=x the 'axis of symmetry.')
y-m-52-02.thinking.0: Examine the conditions under which a generalization holds
y-m-52-02.thinking.1: Build a counterexample that satisfies the conditions
y-m-52-02.thinking.2: Correct the claim using what the counterexamples have in common
y-m-52-02.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level for production assignment; the curriculum does not set a grade for it. It assumes students who have already studied the functions unit of high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-52-02.prereq.1: The meaning of an inverse function, and the fact that the graphs of f and f⁻¹ are symmetric about y=x
y-m-52-02.prereq.2: Graphs of linear functions, solving linear equations
y-m-52-02.s.s1.prompt: The two functions Jiho tested are f(x)=2x−3 and f(x)=x³. What can we say about Jiho's claim from just these two examples?
y-m-52-02.s.s1.hint.0: Picture the graphs of the two functions in words and look for something they have in common.
y-m-52-02.s.s1.hint.1: Think of one example of a linear function that does not have that common feature.
y-m-52-02.s.s1.o.a: Both examples go up. We cannot reach a conclusion before testing a function that goes down.
y-m-52-02.s.s1.r.a: This shows you looked at what features the tested examples share and doubted the cases outside them.
y-m-52-02.s.s1.o.b: We tested two different kinds, a linear and a cubic function, so we have already tested every case.
y-m-52-02.s.s1.r.b: Even if the kinds of function (the form of the expression) differ, their graphs can share the same feature in shape. Compare the shapes of the two graphs.
y-m-52-02.s.s1.o.c: Since the graphs are symmetric, it has already been proved that the intersection points must be on the axis of symmetry.
y-m-52-02.s.s1.r.c: To say where the intersection points are, you must separately consider whether they are on the axis of symmetry or not. Think about whether the fact of symmetry also decides the location of the intersection points.
y-m-52-02.s.s1.o.d: There are as many as 2 examples, so we can practically say it always holds. There is no need to test more.
y-m-52-02.s.s1.r.d: No matter how many examples there are, if you collect only examples of the same kind, they do not guarantee 'always.'
y-m-52-02.s.s1.explain: Both examples are graphs going up to the right. Jiho did not test a graph that goes down, so his check covers only part of the cases.
y-m-52-02.s.s2.prompt: Let f(x)=ax+b (a≠0). Then f⁻¹(x)=(x−b)/a. Find 3 examples, using different combinations of (a, b, x0), where the two graphs meet at a point with x-coordinate x0 but that point is not on the line y=x.
y-m-52-02.s.s2.hint.0: Write f⁻¹(x) as an expression, and write the equation saying that the values of f and f⁻¹ are equal at one point x0.
y-m-52-02.s.s2.hint.1: Change a to -2, -1, 1/2, 2, and so on, and check whether the two values become equal at the same point.
y-m-52-02.s.s2.hint.2: When you gather your three examples, look at whether a or b is always the same value.
y-m-52-02.s.s2.fail.c1: If a=0, there is no inverse function.
y-m-52-02.s.s2.ok.c2: At x=x0 the values of f and f⁻¹ are equal (the two graphs meet).
y-m-52-02.s.s2.fail.c2: At x=x0, f(x0) and f⁻¹(x0) are different from each other. Calculate f⁻¹(x0)=(x0−b)/a directly and compare.
y-m-52-02.s.s2.ok.c3: That intersection point is not on y=x.
y-m-52-02.s.s2.fail.c3: That point is on y=x. Check whether the y-coordinate f(x0) of the intersection is different from x0.
y-m-52-02.s.s2.explain: For example, if f(x)=−x+3, then f⁻¹(x)=3−x=f(x). The two graphs overlap completely, so a point like (0,3), which is not on y=x, is also an intersection point. Simplifying condition c2 gives (a+1)((a−1)x0+b)=0, and if the second factor is 0 then f(x0)=x0, so the point is on y=x; therefore an intersection point off y=x occurs only when a=−1.
y-m-52-02.s.s3.prompt: Write what you see in common among the examples you found, and rewrite Jiho's claim in the form 'it holds under some condition.'
y-m-52-02.s.s3.hint.0: Compare the three combinations (a, b, x0) you found in a table to see which value is the same in all of them.
y-m-52-02.s.s3.hint.1: When a is not −1, solve directly whether the solutions of f(x)=f⁻¹(x) are only points on y=x.
y-m-52-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the value of a was the same in all the examples you found?
y-m-52-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Does your corrected sentence clearly say 'for which kind of function'?
y-m-52-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check that your corrected claim does not contradict the examples you tested (2x−3, x³, etc.)?
y-m-52-02.s.s3.model.0: The examples were all lines with slope −1. If the slope is −1, f and f⁻¹ become the same, so the whole line is intersection points and there are intersection points off y=x too. So we can correct it to say it is right only when f is an increasing function.
y-m-52-02.s.s3.modelNote.0: An answer that states the increasing function condition
y-m-52-02.s.s3.model.1: What they have in common is that a=−1. f(x)=−x+b is its own inverse, so every point is a meeting point. For a function that goes up to the right, it is right to say the intersection points are on y=x.

y-m-52-03.title: The asymptotes and intercept Harin wrote: how far can we trust them?
y-m-52-03.topic: Rewriting a rational function and its graph
y-m-52-03.goal: Find the wrong line in a solution, sort out which of the asymptotes, intercept, and graph position that error affects and which it does not, and suggest a way of checking that lets the error be discovered on one's own.
y-m-52-03.material: To learn about the graph of the rational function y=(2x+1)/(x−1), Harin solved it as below. She wrote that the asymptotes are x=1 and y=2, and she also found the point where this graph meets the y-axis. (Think about real numbers x with x≠1.)
y-m-52-03.thinking.1: Judging how far the error reaches
y-m-52-03.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level for production assignment; the curriculum does not set a grade for it. It assumes students who have already studied the functions unit of high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-52-03.prereq.1: The graph of the rational function y=k/(x−p)+q and its asymptotes (x=p, y=q)
y-m-52-03.prereq.2: Adding and subtracting fractional expressions (the method of dividing the numerator by the denominator)
y-m-52-03.s.s1.prompt: Pick one line in Harin's solution that contains a wrong judgment. (There may be more than one.)
y-m-52-03.s.s1.hint.0: Check one by one whether each line follows from the line just before it.
y-m-52-03.s.s1.line.0: Writing the numerator 2x+1 in a form that contains the denominator x−1, we get 2x+1 = 2(x−1) + 3.
y-m-52-03.s.s1.line.2: The asymptotes are x = 1 and y = 2.
y-m-52-03.s.s1.line.3: Substituting x = 0 gives y = 2 + 1/(0−1) = 1, so the y-intercept is 1.
y-m-52-03.s.s1.line.4: The graph lies in the upper right and lower left of the four regions divided by the two asymptotes.
y-m-52-03.s.s1.explain: In line 2, 3/(x−1) was changed to 1/(x−1) (the 3 was dropped). Line 4 is the result of using that wrong expression, so the y-intercept came out as 1. Substituting x=0 into the original expression gives (0+1)/(0−1)=−1.
y-m-52-03.s.s2.prompt: Pick all the results in Harin's solution that are actually correct regardless of the error.
y-m-52-03.s.s2.hint.0: Compare, for the original expression and for Harin's expression, the x that makes the denominator 0 and the y when x is very large.
y-m-52-03.s.s2.hint.1: Substitute x=0 and x=2 into both expressions and mark the items where the values are the same.
y-m-52-03.s.s2.r.a: The y-intercept is a value obtained by substituting into the expression with the error. Compare it with the value from putting x=0 into the original expression.
y-m-52-03.s.s2.o.b: The asymptotes are x=1 and y=2
y-m-52-03.s.s2.r.b: Asymptotes are determined by the value that makes the denominator 0 and by the constant term. Think about whether they change when the numerator's coefficient changes, as with 3 and 1.
y-m-52-03.s.s2.o.c: The graph passes through the point (2, 3)
y-m-52-03.s.s2.r.c: This is the value from putting x=2 into Harin's expression. Compare it with the value from putting x=2 into the original expression.
y-m-52-03.s.s2.o.d: The graph lies in the upper right and lower left regions
y-m-52-03.s.s2.r.d: The sign of the constant 3 in the numerator decides the regions. Think about whether the regions are the same because both 1 and 3 are positive.
y-m-52-03.s.s2.explain: The asymptotes (x=1, y=2) and the regions where the graph lies do not change even if 3 becomes 1 (both are positive). But the y-intercept and the points it passes through change in value and are wrong: in the original expression the y-intercept is −1, and when x=2, y=5.
y-m-52-03.s.s3.prompt: Write a note that does not give the correct answer right away but suggests one way of checking, so that Harin can check on her own whether her expression y=2+1/(x−1) equals the original expression.
y-m-52-03.s.s3.hint.0: Put the same x into the original expression and Harin's expression and write the values side by side.
y-m-52-03.s.s3.hint.1: First remember that you cannot put 1 in for x.
y-m-52-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does your note suggest a checking action, without directly saying the right answer (that it should be 3)?
y-m-52-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you try the suggested check yourself and find that it reveals the error?
y-m-52-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Is the tone one that a friend receiving it can understand?
y-m-52-03.s.s3.model.0: If I put x=2 into the original expression I get 5, but if I put x=2 into your expression I get 3. If the two expressions were equal, they should give the same value, so please look again line by line at where it changed.
y-m-52-03.s.s3.model.1: Try combining your 2+1/(x−1) over a common denominator into a single fraction. If you compare it with the original expression (2x+1)/(x−1), you will be able to see where it went wrong.
y-m-52-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: The method of combining over a common denominator and comparing with the original expression

y-m-52-04.title: If we don't know k, how many times does it meet the x-axis?
y-m-52-04.topic: Intersections of a quadratic function's graph with the x-axis
y-m-52-04.goal: Experience how the judgment about the number of intersection points of a quadratic function with the x-axis narrows as information increases, and state all the possible cases even when some value is unknown.
y-m-52-04.material: There is a parabola y = x² − 4x + k (k is a constant). Information about k is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose what you can say about the number of points where this parabola meets the x-axis (count a point where it just touches as 1 point).
y-m-52-04.thinking.0: Considering all possible cases when information is lacking
y-m-52-04.thinking.1: Narrowing or changing a judgment with new information
y-m-52-04.thinking.2: Finding several values that fit a condition
y-m-52-04.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level for production assignment; the curriculum does not set a grade for it. It assumes students who have already studied the functions unit of high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-52-04.prereq.1: Graphs of quadratic functions (vertex, opening upward), and the relation between real roots of a quadratic equation and the points where the graph meets the x-axis
y-m-52-04.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. Choose your judgment each time.
y-m-52-04.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, explain in words where the vertex of the parabola is (above or below the x-axis).
y-m-52-04.s.s1.hint.1: Put a few small integers in for k and organize the number of intersection points in a table.
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.0.info: You do not know k, but you know only that k is positive (k>0).
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: What can we say about the number of points where this parabola meets the x-axis?
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.0.after: Since y=(x−2)²+k−4, the vertex is (2, k−4). If 0<k<4 the vertex is below the x-axis, so there are 2 points; if k=4 it touches the x-axis, so 1 point; if k>4 it is above the x-axis, so 0 points. When there is an unknown value, you have to consider all the possible cases.
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Since k is positive, the vertex is above the x-axis, so there are always 0 meeting points
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Write the y-coordinate of the vertex directly in terms of k. 'k is positive' is not the same as 'the y-coordinate of the vertex is positive.'
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: A parabola that opens upward always has 2 points
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Even if it opens upward, if the parabola floats completely above the x-axis, it does not meet it. Think about the position of the vertex.
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Depending on the value of k, 0, 1, and 2 points are all possible
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is a judgment that considers the possible cases by picturing the y-coordinate of the vertex moving up and down with k.
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Only 0 or 2 are possible, and there is no k that gives exactly 1
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: 1 point happens when the vertex lies on the x-axis. Check whether such a k is among the positive numbers.
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.1.info: New fact: the y-coordinate of the vertex of this parabola is 0 or less.
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: Combined with the information k>0, what can we say about the number of meeting points?
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.1.after: If k−4≤0 and k>0, then 0<k≤4. If 0<k<4, there are two different points, and if k=4, it touches at one point. So 0 points is impossible, but we still do not know whether it is 1 or 2. The first judgment ('all are possible') was not wrong; as information increased, the possible cases decreased.
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It is 1 or 2 depending on whether k is 4, and it meets at at least one point
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This is a judgment that separates the case where the y-coordinate of the vertex is 0 from the case where it is less than 0.
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Regardless of the position of the vertex, 0, 1, and 2 points are still all possible
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Write again how the condition that the y-coordinate k−4 of the vertex is 0 or less narrowed the range of possible k.
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: If we do not know whether k is exactly 4, we cannot decide whether it is 1 or 2, but it is not 0
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is a judgment that separates what cannot be decided from what can be decided.
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Since the vertex is below the x-axis, it is always decided to be 2
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Check whether the case where the y-coordinate of the vertex is exactly 0 is included in the condition.
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.2.info: You also learn that k is an integer. (an integer k with 0<k≤4)
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: How many values of k make the x-coordinates of all the points where it meets the x-axis integers?
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.2.after: If k=1, x=2±√3, and if k=2, x=2±√2, which are not integers. If k=3, x=1, 3, and if k=4, x=2 (the touching point), which are all integers, so the answer is 2. Depending on whether the touching case is counted as an intersection, the answer could be read as 1, so at the start we agreed 'count it as 1 intersection point.'
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: A touching case (1 intersection point) is also an intersection point. Look back at whether you checked that the x-coordinate in that case is an integer.
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This is the judgment that matches the result of substituting the four values of k in turn and finding the x-coordinates of the intersection points.
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Find directly the x-coordinates of the intersection points for k=1 and 2.
y-m-52-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Find directly the x-coordinates of the points where it meets the x-axis when k=1 and check whether they are integers.
y-m-52-04.s.s1.reflect: At first you judged 'all are possible,' but as information increased it narrowed to 'not 0' and 'only 2 as a candidate.' How is your judgment changing different from your first judgment being wrong? If you had settled on one number with too little information, where would you have been wrong?
y-m-52-04.s.s2.prompt: This time, there is no condition that k is positive; only that k is an integer. Find 3 different values of k for which the parabola meets the x-axis at two different points and the distance between those two points is an integer.
y-m-52-04.s.s2.hint.0: Fix one k and find the x-coordinates of the two intersection points.
y-m-52-04.s.s2.hint.1: Write the distance between the two intersection points in terms of k, and look at what form k must have for that value to be an integer.
y-m-52-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Please enter k as an integer.
y-m-52-04.s.s2.ok.c2: It meets at two different points.
y-m-52-04.s.s2.fail.c2: For this k it does not meet at two different points. Check whether the vertex is below the x-axis.
y-m-52-04.s.s2.ok.c3: The distance between the two intersection points is an integer.
y-m-52-04.s.s2.fail.c3: The distance between the two intersection points is not an integer. Find the x-coordinates of the two intersection points and check their difference.
y-m-52-04.s.s2.explain: The x-coordinates of the two intersection points are 2±√(4−k), so the distance is 2√(4−k). If 4−k is a perfect square (1, 4, 9, 16, ...), the distance is an integer, and k = 3, 0, −5, −12, −21, ...

y-m-52-05.title: Where did Doyun's solution go off track?
y-m-52-05.topic: Minimum of a quadratic function on an interval, and a parameter
y-m-52-05.goal: Learn that the assumption 'the minimum of a quadratic function on an interval occurs at the vertex' may not hold, then split into cases to find the value of the parameter and check that the value satisfies the assumption.
y-m-52-05.material:
Doyun solved the following problem. (a is a constant, and x is a real number with 0 ≤ x ≤ 3)
Problem: Find the value of a such that the minimum of f(x) = x² − 2ax on 0 ≤ x ≤ 3 is −12.
Doyun's solution is below.
y-m-52-05.thinking.0: Finding the hidden assumption in the solution
y-m-52-05.thinking.2: Checking that the value found fits the assumption
y-m-52-05.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level for production assignment; the curriculum does not set a grade for it. It assumes students who have already studied the functions unit of high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-52-05.prereq.1: Standard form of a quadratic function (completing the square), maximum and minimum on an interval
y-m-52-05.prereq.2: Calculating with expressions in which the unknown is written as the letter a
y-m-52-05.s.s1.prompt: Pick one line in Doyun's solution that contains a wrong judgment. (There may be more than one.)
y-m-52-05.s.s1.hint.0: Check with numbers whether the x-coordinate a of the vertex is inside or outside the interval [0, 3].
y-m-52-05.s.s1.hint.1: When a=2√3, calculate the values of f(0) and f(3) and compare them with −12.
y-m-52-05.s.s1.line.0: f(x) = x² − 2ax = (x − a)² − a², so the vertex is (a, −a²).
y-m-52-05.s.s1.line.1: The minimum on the interval 0 ≤ x ≤ 3 is −12, so −a² = −12 must hold.
y-m-52-05.s.s1.line.3: Therefore the values of a that satisfy the condition are 2√3 and −2√3.
y-m-52-05.s.s1.explain: In line 2, it was assumed that the minimum occurs at the vertex, but this is right only when the x-coordinate a of the vertex is between 0 and 3 inclusive. In line 4, it was not checked whether the a found satisfies that assumption. 2√3≈3.46 and −2√3≈−3.46 are both outside the interval [0,3].
y-m-52-05.s.s2.prompt: We want to fix Doyun's solution. When a=5, what is the minimum of f(x)=x²−10x on the interval 0 ≤ x ≤ 3?
y-m-52-05.s.s2.hint.0: Substitute x=0, 1, 2, 3 in turn and make a table to see how the values change.
y-m-52-05.s.s2.hint.1: In the table, check at which x the smallest value appeared.
y-m-52-05.s.s2.r.a: This is the value you get by leaving out the x² term and calculating only −10x. Calculate f(3) again from the start.
y-m-52-05.s.s2.r.b: This used the vertex value −a² as it is. First check whether the x-coordinate 5 of the vertex is inside the interval.
y-m-52-05.s.s2.r.c: This is a judgment that found the point inside the interval where the value is smallest and found the value of f there.
y-m-52-05.s.s2.r.d: This is the value at x=0. Compare which of the two ends of the interval gives the smaller value.
y-m-52-05.s.s2.explain: If a=5, the x-coordinate 5 of the vertex is outside the interval. Within the interval f keeps decreasing, so the minimum is at x=3 and f(3)=9−30=−21.
y-m-52-05.s.s3.prompt: Now find the correct a and enter it. (The a for which the minimum of f(x)=x²−2ax on the interval 0 ≤ x ≤ 3 is exactly −12. Write fractions as decimals.)
y-m-52-05.s.s3.hint.0: Split into the cases where a is less than 0, inside the interval, and greater than 3, and write where the minimum occurs in each case.
y-m-52-05.s.s3.hint.1: In each case find the a that makes the minimum −12, then check whether that a satisfies the condition of the case.
y-m-52-05.s.s3.ok.c1: The minimum of f on the interval [0,3] is −12.
y-m-52-05.s.s3.fail.c1: For this a, the minimum on the interval [0,3] is not −12. Split into the cases where a is inside the interval, to the left, and to the right, and find the minimum again.
y-m-52-05.s.s3.explain: If a<0, f is increasing on the interval, so the minimum is f(0)=0; if 0≤a≤3, the minimum is −a² at the vertex (to get −12 we need a²=12, but 3.46>3, so it is impossible); if a>3, f is decreasing, so the minimum is f(3)=9−6a=−12, which gives a=7/2. The only a that satisfies the condition is 7/2.
y-m-52-05.s.s3.because.prompt: Explain with numbers why a=2√3, which Doyun found, does not satisfy the condition.
y-m-52-05.s.s3.because.hint.0: Approximate 2√3 as a decimal and compare it with the interval [0,3].
y-m-52-05.s.s3.because.hint.1: Calculate directly the value at x=3 for that a.
y-m-52-05.s.s3.because.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation include numbers (the size of 2√3 or values of f)?
y-m-52-05.s.s3.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say that where the minimum occurs differs depending on whether the vertex is inside or outside the interval?
y-m-52-05.s.s3.because.model.0: 2√3 is about 3.46, so it is outside the interval 0 to 3. If the vertex is outside the interval, the minimum occurs not at the vertex but at the endpoint x=3, so we must not use the vertex value −12.
y-m-52-05.s.s3.because.model.1: If a=2√3, the vertex is at x=3.46, so it is not in the interval. In fact, at x=3, f(3)=9−12√3≈−11.8, so the minimum is not −12.
y-m-52-05.s.s3.because.modelNote.1: An answer that refuted it with actual values

y-m-52-06.title: How many times do a curve and a line meet?
y-m-52-06.topic: Number of intersections of an irrational function's graph and a line
y-m-52-06.goal: Learn that the number of intersections of an irrational function and a line cannot be decided by the discriminant of a quadratic equation alone, and find on your own the range of k for which there are exactly 2 intersections by considering the domain and range of values (x+k−1≥0).
y-m-52-06.material:
The graph of the irrational function y = √(x+2) + 1 is a curve that starts at the point (−2, 1) and rises to the upper right, gradually flattening (x ≥ −2). We want to find the number of intersections with the line y = x + k.
Daeun solved it like this. “Set the two expressions equal to get √(x+2) = x + k − 1, then square both sides to get x² + (2k−3)x + (k−1)² − 2 = 0. The discriminant of this quadratic equation is 13 − 4k, so if k < 13/4 there are two different real roots, which means two intersections.”
y-m-52-06.thinking.0: Checking the limits of the solving method
y-m-52-06.thinking.1: Checking whether the solutions found satisfy the original expression
y-m-52-06.thinking.2: Making several values that fit a condition
y-m-52-06.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level for production assignment; the curriculum does not set a grade for it. It assumes students who have already studied the functions unit of high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-52-06.prereq.1: The graph of the irrational function y=√(x+p)+q (domain, starting point)
y-m-52-06.prereq.2: Roots and discriminant of a quadratic equation, and the habit of checking that the roots satisfy the original expression
y-m-52-06.s.s1.prompt: When k=0, Daeun's quadratic equation is x² − 3x − 1 = 0, and its two roots are about 3.30 and −0.30. Substitute the two roots into the original expression √(x+2) = x − 1. What is your judgment about Daeun's conclusion (two intersections)?
y-m-52-06.s.s1.hint.0: Substitute each of the two roots into √(x+2) and x−1 and write the two values side by side.
y-m-52-06.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the signs of the two values are the same.
y-m-52-06.s.s1.o.a: It is not right. Of the two roots, −0.30 makes the right side of the original expression negative, so it does not satisfy it, and there is one intersection.
y-m-52-06.s.s1.r.a: This is a judgment that substituted the roots into the original expression and checked even the signs of both sides.
y-m-52-06.s.s1.o.b: It is right. The quadratic equation has two roots and they are inside the domain x ≥ −2, so there are two intersections.
y-m-52-06.s.s1.r.b: You only checked that the roots are inside the domain. Check again whether the signs of both sides of the original expression also fit.
y-m-52-06.s.s1.o.c: It is not right. The quadratic equation has no roots, so there are 0 intersections.
y-m-52-06.s.s1.r.c: The equation x²−3x−1=0 does have real roots. The question is whether those roots satisfy the original expression.
y-m-52-06.s.s1.o.d: It is not right, but the cause is the domain. x = −0.30 is fine because x ≥ −2, so one root is a calculation mistake.
y-m-52-06.s.s1.r.d: x=−0.30 is inside the domain. Look for another cause and compare the results of substituting into the original expression.
y-m-52-06.s.s1.explain: √(x+2) is 0 or more, so x−1 must also be 0 or more. If x=−0.30, then x−1=−1.30<0, so it does not satisfy √(x+2)=x−1 (a false root created in the process of squaring both sides). At k=0 the only actual intersection is the one at x≈3.30.
y-m-52-06.s.s2.prompt: Find 3 different values of k for which the line y = x + k and the curve y = √(x+2) + 1 meet at two different points. (You may enter decimals.)
y-m-52-06.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a few values of k and picture in words the shape of the curve and the line (imagine moving the line up and down).
y-m-52-06.s.s2.hint.1: Find the k for which the line passes through the starting point (−2,1) of the curve.
y-m-52-06.s.s2.hint.2: Count and compare the number of intersections directly for k=3 and k=2.9.
y-m-52-06.s.s2.fail.c1: For this k the number of intersections is not 2. Think about whether the line is above or below the starting point (−2, 1) of the curve, and when the moment it touches the curve comes.
y-m-52-06.s.s2.explain: Letting t=√(x+2) (t≥0), the points where y=x+k meets the curve y=√(x+2)+1 correspond to the roots t≥0 of k=−t²+t+3, one point per root. On t≥0, −t²+t+3 equals 3 at t=0 and has maximum 13/4 at t=1/2, so if 3≤k<13/4 there are 2 intersections, if k=13/4 it touches and there is 1, if k<3 there is 1, and if k>13/4 there are 0. For example, if k=3 they meet at (−2,1) and (−1,2).
y-m-52-06.s.s3.prompt: When you slowly raise the line y=x+k from far below, there are two moments when the number of intersections changes. Explain where the line and the curve are located at each of those moments.
y-m-52-06.s.s3.hint.0: Find k when the line passes through the starting point (−2,1).
y-m-52-06.s.s3.hint.1: Imagine the moment when, as you raise the line once more, it just barely touches the curve.
y-m-52-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you explain the positions of the line and the curve in words for both moments?
y-m-52-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you connect them with the values of k (3, 13/4)?
y-m-52-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you compare the number of intersections before and after each moment?
y-m-52-06.s.s3.model.0: As you raise the line, first at the moment it passes the starting point (−2,1) of the curve (k=3), the intersections increase from 1 to 2. If you raise it more, at the moment it touches the curve (k=13/4) it becomes 1, and after that it is 0.
y-m-52-06.s.s3.model.1: At first it meets the curve at one point, and when the line passes the left endpoint it becomes two points. As it keeps rising, it grazes the curve once and leaves, and they do not meet.
y-m-52-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that explains by positions without numbers

y-m-52-08.title: How many correspondences make the values go up?
y-m-52-08.topic: Counting functions and correspondences that satisfy a condition
y-m-52-08.goal: Build functions that satisfy the condition 'f(1)<f(2)<f(3)' yourself, compare different ways of counting them, and judge how the condition changes the count.
y-m-52-08.material: We want to count the functions f from the set X={1, 2, 3} to the set Y={1, 2, 3, 4, 5} that satisfy f(1) < f(2) < f(3). (f(1), f(2), and f(3) are each elements of Y.)
y-m-52-08.thinking.0: Comparing whether the ways of counting are valid
y-m-52-08.thinking.1: Building correspondences that fit the condition yourself
y-m-52-08.thinking.2: Predicting how the count changes when the condition is weakened
y-m-52-08.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level for production assignment; the curriculum does not set a grade for it. It assumes students who have already studied the functions unit of high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-52-08.prereq.1: The meaning of a function (each element of the domain corresponds to exactly one element of the codomain)
y-m-52-08.prereq.2: The product rule and basic ideas of permutations and combinations
y-m-52-08.s.s1.prompt: Four friends counted in different ways. Pick all the ways that count correctly.
y-m-52-08.s.s1.hint.0: Pick 3 elements of Y and write out all the f you can make with those values.
y-m-52-08.s.s1.hint.1: Take {1,2,3} as an example and compare Seoyun's method with the condition f(1)<f(2)<f(3).
y-m-52-08.s.s1.o.a: Hajun: f(1), f(2), and f(3) can each be chosen freely in 5 ways, so 5×5×5=125.
y-m-52-08.s.s1.r.a: 125 is the number counting all functions without any condition. Think about how much the condition f(1)<f(2)<f(3) reduces the count.
y-m-52-08.s.s1.o.b: Seoyun: f(1) has 5 ways, f(2) has 4 ways among the remaining values, and f(3) has 3 ways among the remaining values, so 5×4×3=60.
y-m-52-08.s.s1.r.b: 5×4×3 is the number of ways to line up 'three different values in order.' Think about how many of the different arrangements of the same three values satisfy the condition.
y-m-52-08.s.s1.o.c: Jihu: If you pick three different values, they are decided as f(1), f(2), f(3) from smallest, so 10.
y-m-52-08.s.s1.r.c: This is a judgment that thought about whether picking three different values decides exactly one arrangement that satisfies the condition.
y-m-52-08.s.s1.o.d: Naeun: Of Seoyun's 60, among the 6 arrangements of the same three values only 1 is increasing, so 60÷6=10.
y-m-52-08.s.s1.r.d: This is a judgment that connected the number of arrangements of three different values with the proportion of them that satisfy the condition.
y-m-52-08.s.s1.explain: If you pick three different values {p<q<r}, one increasing function f(1)=p, f(2)=q, f(3)=r is decided, and this is a one-to-one correspondence with all increasing functions. So 5C3=10. Seoyun's 60 counts every arrangement of the same three values in 6 orders, so you can also get it as 60÷6=10.
y-m-52-08.s.s2.prompt: Build functions that satisfy the condition f(1) < f(2) < f(3) as 4 different ordered triples (f(1), f(2), f(3)). (a=f(1), b=f(2), c=f(3), all integers from 1 to 5)
y-m-52-08.s.s2.hint.0: Decide the smallest possible value of f(1) first, then write down in turn the values f(2) and f(3) can take.
y-m-52-08.s.s2.hint.1: Add them to your list one at a time so that they do not overlap with the ordered triples you already made.
y-m-52-08.s.s2.fail.c1: Please enter all three values as integers.
y-m-52-08.s.s2.ok.c2: All three values are from 1 to 5.
y-m-52-08.s.s2.fail.c2: You can only use elements of Y={1, 2, 3, 4, 5}.
y-m-52-08.s.s2.fail.c3: The values are not in an increasing order. Choose again so that f(1)<f(2)<f(3).
y-m-52-08.s.s3.prompt: If we change the condition to f(1) ≤ f(2) ≤ f(3), will the number of functions that satisfy it be more than 10, fewer, or the same? Explain the reason with an example.
y-m-52-08.s.s3.hint.0: Write one function that satisfies the new condition but not the previous condition.
y-m-52-08.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether the functions that satisfied the previous condition also satisfy the new condition.
y-m-52-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write at least one example yourself of a function that is newly allowed?
y-m-52-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that the first 10 are all still included?
y-m-52-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Even without counting the increased number exactly, did you explain in words the reason why it increases?
y-m-52-08.s.s3.model.0: It increases. Since equal values are allowed, as in f(1)=f(2), new cases like (1,1,2) or (2,2,2) appear, and the original 10 are still included.
y-m-52-08.s.s3.model.1: It gets bigger. Since values may be equal, (3,3,5) works and (4,4,4) works too. The 10 with f(1)<f(2)<f(3) from before also all satisfy the new condition, so there are more than 10.
y-m-52-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: An answer that says the earlier 10 are included

y-m-52-09.title: When two models pass through the same points, which should we trust?
y-m-52-09.topic: Comparing an inverse proportion model and a linear model
y-m-52-09.goal: Judge, step by step with new measurements, which of two models that both fit two points to trust, while considering the range in which a model can be used and measurement error.
y-m-52-09.thinking.1: Judging the range in which a model can be used
y-m-52-09.thinking.2: Interpreting the difference between a measurement and a prediction
y-m-52-09.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level for production assignment; the curriculum does not set a grade for it. It assumes students who have already studied the functions unit of high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-52-09.prereq.1: Graphs and expressions of linear and inverse proportion functions, the relation among speed, distance, and time
y-m-52-09.s.s1.prompt: Measurements are added one at a time. Each time, choose which model to trust and how.
y-m-52-09.s.s1.hint.0: Put 20 km, 25 km, and 30 km per hour into each model and compare the predicted values in a table.
y-m-52-09.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate the difference between the predicted values and the measured values and compare the two models.
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.0.info: The only data known now are the two measurements (72 minutes at 10 km per hour, 48 minutes at 15 km per hour).
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.0.ask: If you ride at 20 km per hour, how many minutes do you expect it to take?
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The predictions of the two models are different, so we cannot decide from this data alone. We need to measure at 20 km per hour
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This is a judgment that admits the data cannot tell which model is right and decides what information to get next.
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.0.o.b: 24 minutes. The line through two points is the simplest model, so we trust that line as it is
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.0.o.d: 30 minutes. The midpoint of 24 and 36 minutes has the smallest error whichever side is wrong
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.0.r.d: The average of the two models is a value that neither model predicts. The value is decided by which model you trust.
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.1.info: If you put 30 km per hour into Model A, you get −24 minutes, and if you put it into Model B, you get 24 minutes.
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.1.ask: What would you judge about Model A?
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.1.after: At 25 km per hour, Model A's time becomes 0 minutes, and above that it is negative. So A can be used only in the range where the speed is 25 or less. B gives positive values for all positive speeds, but that is not evidence that B is right, and it has to be confirmed with new measurements.
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.1.o.a: B also has the problem that the time approaches 0 as the speed gets larger, so the two models are equally unsuitable
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.1.r.a: No matter how large the speed gets, B's time stays positive. Compare whether it is the same problem as A, whose time becomes 0 or negative.
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.1.o.b: A negative time is impossible, so A cannot be used when the speed is over 25 km/h. We have to limit the range
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This is a judgment that considered the range in which the model can give real-world values.
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It has only been confirmed that A cannot be used in this range; whether B is right has to be confirmed with new measurements
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is a judgment that distinguishes between a flaw being revealed and the other model being confirmed as right.
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It has been confirmed that A has a problem, so it is practically settled that the inverse proportion model B is the right model
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.1.r.d: A flaw in one model is not evidence that the other model is right. Think about whether there are parts of B that have not been tested yet.
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.2.ask: Looking at the measurement, what would you do about Model B?
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.2.after: The difference between Model B's prediction and the measurement is 1 minute, and for Model A it is 13 minutes. A small difference can be explained by measuring conditions such as waiting at a traffic light, so it is reasonable to keep B. Still, measuring again under the same conditions would make it more certain.
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The difference between 36 and 37 minutes is small and is explained by the traffic light wait, so we keep B while allowing for the error
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This is a judgment that looked at the size of the difference, considered a factor outside the data (waiting at the light), and kept the model.
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.2.o.b: B predicted 36 minutes but the actual was 37 minutes, so it is a wrong model and we throw it away and make a new one
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.2.r.b: If you throw away a model because prediction and measurement are not exactly the same, you will throw away almost every model. Think about the size and the cause of the difference.
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The difference between prediction and measurement is much smaller for B (1 minute versus 13 minutes). The effect of the traffic light wait can be checked by measuring again
y-m-52-09.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This is a judgment that compared the size of the differences with numbers and suggested an additional measurement.
y-m-52-09.s.s1.reflect: At first it was hard to tell which model was right, but as new information accumulated, the range in which A can be used narrowed and B was close to the measurement. Each time information was added, how did you tell apart 'what was confirmed' and 'what has not yet been confirmed'?
y-m-52-09.s.s2.prompt: For Model B (time = 720 ÷ speed), find 3 different pairs (v, t) in which the speed (km per hour) and the time (minutes) are both integers from 5 to 60.
y-m-52-09.s.s2.hint.0: Check whether the pair you already know, (15,48), satisfies the condition, then make other pairs in the same way.
y-m-52-09.s.s2.hint.1: First think about what should happen to the time if you double the speed.
y-m-52-09.s.s2.ok.c1: v and t are both integers.
y-m-52-09.s.s2.fail.c1: Please enter the speed and time as integers.
y-m-52-09.s.s2.ok.c2: v and t are both from 5 to 60.
y-m-52-09.s.s2.fail.c2: Please make v and t from 5 to 60.
y-m-52-09.s.s2.ok.c3: It is a pair that fits Model B.
y-m-52-09.s.s2.fail.c3: This pair does not fit Model B (time = 720 ÷ speed). Multiply v and t.
y-m-52-09.s.s2.because.prompt: Calculate the product of speed and time for each of the three pairs you found, and write what you discovered in one sentence.
y-m-52-09.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the value of speed times time for each of the three pairs.
y-m-52-09.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare whether the products are all the same.
y-m-52-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you actually calculate the products of the three pairs?
y-m-52-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you connect what you discovered with the expression of Model B (time=720÷speed)?
y-m-52-09.s.s2.because.model.0: 12×60=720, 20×36=720, 30×24=720: in all three pairs, the product of speed and time is a constant 720.
y-m-52-09.s.s2.because.model.1: The products were all the same, 720. When the speed doubles, the time is halved, so the product always stays the same.
y-m-52-09.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: An answer explained by the rate of change of speed and time

y-m-52-10.title: If we don't know a, is there a maximum?
y-m-52-10.topic: Existence of the maximum of a quadratic function depending on a parameter
y-m-52-10.goal: Learn that the kind of expression can change depending on the value of the unknown constant a, judge what information is needed for a maximum to exist, and find the a that satisfies the condition yourself.
y-m-52-10.material: There is a function f(x) = (a − 1)x² + 4x + 1. a is a real constant, and x is any real number. Seunghun said, “Since it's a quadratic function, it must have either a maximum or a minimum,” and the value of a is not yet known.
y-m-52-10.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
y-m-52-10.thinking.1: Looking separately at the case where the kind of expression changes
y-m-52-10.thinking.2: Making several values that fit a condition
y-m-52-10.prereq.0: H3 in this task is only a difficulty level for production assignment; the curriculum does not set a grade for it. It assumes students who have already studied the functions unit of high school Common Mathematics.
y-m-52-10.prereq.1: Maximum and minimum of a quadratic function (completing the square), the coefficient of the quadratic term and the shape of the graph
y-m-52-10.prereq.2: Graphs of linear functions (the case with no maximum or minimum)
y-m-52-10.s.s1.prompt: What information would we need to judge whether f has a maximum (over all real numbers x)?
y-m-52-10.s.s1.hint.0: Put values like 0, 1, 2 in for a, write f(x), and explain the shape of the graph in words.
y-m-52-10.s.s1.hint.1: Look for an a that makes the coefficient of x² in the expression equal to 0.
y-m-52-10.s.s1.o.a: We need to know whether a is positive or negative. Its sign decides the direction the graph curves
y-m-52-10.s.s1.r.a: The coefficient of the quadratic term is not a but a−1. Write again what value decides whether the coefficient is positive or negative.
y-m-52-10.s.s1.o.b: It is already enough. Since it is a quadratic function, there must be a maximum
y-m-52-10.s.s1.r.b: Check whether there is an a that makes the coefficient a−1 equal to 0. What kind of function would the function be in that case?
y-m-52-10.s.s1.explain: If a−1<0, it is a quadratic function that opens downward, so it has a maximum; if a−1>0, it opens upward, so there is no maximum (only a minimum); and if a=1, f(x)=4x+1 is a linear function, so there is neither a maximum nor a minimum. So we need to know where a is compared with 1.
y-m-52-10.s.s2.prompt: Find 3 different values of a for which f has a maximum and that maximum is 5 or more. (You may enter decimals.)

y-m-52-10.s.s2.explain: For f(x)=(a−1)x²+4x+1, if a<1 the maximum is 1−4/(a−1)=1+4/(1−a). For this to be 5 or more, 4/(1−a)≥4, that is 0<1−a≤1, so 0≤a<1. For example, if a=0 the maximum is 5, if a=0.5 it is 9, and if a=0.9 it is 41.
